e-4838.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
e-4838.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given below. What is $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}?$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/0dce1fb65e0b82525b6d461b3641b10eb6d3641f590d46af6fa4af9f2e020dc6.png)
e-4838.worked_solution:
Given the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-4840.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
e-4840.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ to $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ is given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} =2\mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/acdc98dc5a658e7c945dca00c1a1c0a73d87e3dc98db8071a534a4fd7f215c90.png)
e-4840.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} .
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)(-4)-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 2 \mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/883431c76485c9fd706fe79c2bf3936946cfb0dba602ebd0df77d6cc9e800665.png)

Now, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-4841.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
e-4841.problem:
The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/0dcc93449ac1d14e51850e4a74f639aeb3acd21b720ba2b9deeb2208d9fffeb4.png)
e-4841.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} .
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/50bbd2dd0fa1c0732a01d07c2614ab15549272fcc0b7d686651f0464b3b50f39.png)

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 10-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-7276.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in Another Basis
e-7276.problem:
The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/c6c10ed068cfde656d178c98eb4af979563efc82d589f750b8fa92973f362e2a.png)
e-7276.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/034a2a4079120d719f9061c339899f9aed9b50a765200291ca15c500ef647a70.png)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 13 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & 15 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/8d07812ea170bcbb56264468f4cfd0fa8b88cf4f68f9b50d35f61e9e33de45c3.png)

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & 15 \\ -5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3},$ we have 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 12 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3},$ we have 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 12 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since [x]_B=(3,1,5), multiply by the change-of-coordinates matrix: [x]_C=(3+1+5,3+5,-9+1+15)=(9,8,7). Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=3{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=3{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3},$ we have

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 8 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=3{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=3{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3},$ we have

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 8 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, notice that since x=4b3−2b1, we have

[x]B=[−204].

Given the coordinates of x relative to B and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C, we find the coordinates of x relative to C as follows:

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 7 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=4{b}_{3}-2{b}_{1}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=4{b}_{3}-2{b}_{1},$ we have

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 7 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -14 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis B to the basis C and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the basis B are given below. What is [x]C?

PB→C=[−2−2−13],[x]B=[5−4]

a
[−1−7]
b
[−2−17]
c
[−17−2]
d
[−12−17]
e
[−21]
Submit

decision.explanation: Use [x]_C=P_{B\to C}[x]_B. The coordinates are (-2(5)-2(-4),-1(5)+3(-4))=(-2,-17), so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given below. What is $[x]_{C}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=5{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-{b}_{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=5{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-{b}_{3},$ we have

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

PB→C=[1240−131−31]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis B={b1,b2,b3} to the basis C={c1,c2,c3} is given above. Find [x]C given that x=5b1+b2−b3.

EXPLANATION

First, notice that since x=5b1+b2−b3, we have

[x]B=[51−1].

Given the coordinates of x relative to B and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C, we find the coordinates of x relative to C as follows:

[x]C=PB→C[x]B=[1240−131−31][51−1]=[3−41]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=5{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-{b}_{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=5{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-{b}_{3},$ we have

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-5)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B={b1,b2} to C={c1,c2} is given below. Find [x]B given that x=3c1−3c2.

PB→C=[2−5−13]

a
[−6−3]
b
[−36]
c
[48]
d
[−9−8]
e
[−2−4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[2−5−13]−1=12⋅3−(−1)⋅(−5)[3512]=[3512]

Notice that since x=3c1−3c2, we obtain [x]C=[3−3].

Now, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[3512][3−3]=[−6−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-5)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-8)-(-3)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-8)-(-3)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:

$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 6-5\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}6 & -5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=-3{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[4556]−1=14⋅6−5⋅5[6−5−54]=[−655−4]

Notice that since x=−3c1−5c2, we obtain [x]C=[−3−5].

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[−655−4][−3−5]=[−75]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=-3{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 6-5\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}6 & -5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=-3{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given below. What is $[x]_{B}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]

after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given below. What is $[x]_{B}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}22 \\ 35\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given below. What is $[x]_{B}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-4)-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 2-1\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 2-1\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 3-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{5}{3} & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{5}{3} & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}15 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

B={[65],[33]},[x]S=[1510]

The basis B of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the standard basis S are given above. Find [x]B.

a
[5−5]
b
[53]
c
[15−5]
d
[3−4]
e
[31]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[6353].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[6353]−1=16⋅3−3⋅5[3−3−56]=[1−1−532]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[1−1−532][1510]=[5−5]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 3-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{5}{3} & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{5}{3} & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}15 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}7 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-4)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ -2 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[−1−4−2−7][22]=[−10−18]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}7 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-4)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ -2 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ -2 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 3-11\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[41113].

PS→B=PB→S−1=[41113]−1=14⋅3−11⋅1[3−1−114]=[3−1−114]

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[3−1−114][25]=[1−2]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 11\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 3-11\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[5−7−36].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[5−7−36]−1=15⋅6−(−7)⋅(−3)[6735]=[23791359]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[23791359][18−9]=[51]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 13 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in Another Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 13 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 1 \\ -6 & 19 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 22 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}22 & 19 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}22 & 19 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 10\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & 10 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 18 & -29 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}18 & -29 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -29 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}].
$$

 

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 5 & 6 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -6 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ 5 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 7 \\ 5 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
